items.text: THE BREAKERS - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design THE BREAKERS Palm Beach, FL, United States Tihany Design has gone on to breathe new life into a number of venues across the property in the ongoing renovation of the iconic Palm Beach resort. In addition to HMF, Tihany-designed spaces include The Lobby, The Flagler Steakhouse, Seafood Bar, Flagler Club Lounge, the South Oceanfront Tower guest rooms and suites and the specialty suites Royal Poinciana and Imperial. From dining venues to guest rooms, the new design maintains the integrity of the historic property while infusing each space with a renewed sense of Palm Beach sophistication and spirit. ___________________ HOTEL GUEST ROOMS & SUITES PUBLIC SPACES RESTAURANTS ___________________ CLIENT, OPERATOR The Breakers Palm Beach ﻿visit website﻿ Photo Eric Laignel; Riccardo Piazza Previous DANIEL Next BOUCHON BISTRO NEW YORK 135 West 27th Street New York, NY 10001 t. +1 212 366 5544 LEGAL privacy policy cookie policy copyright © Tihany Design

items.title: THE PENROSE ROOM - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design
items.text: THE PENROSE ROOM - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design THE PENROSE ROOM Colorado Springs, CO, United States Set within The Broadmoor in Colorado Springs, The Penrose Room reimagines one of America’s most storied dining destinations through a layered interior narrative shaped by legacy, landscape, and cultural exchange. Founded in 1918 by Spencer and Julie Penrose, the resort’s spirit of adventure and refined European influence informs a design approach that bridges Old World elegance with the mythology of the American West. Working in close dialogue with this heritage, Tihany Design conceived a sequence of richly detailed environments, from an intimate arrival foyer to a lounge inspired by the conviviality of the Western saloon, reinterpreted through warm wood tones, leather detailing, and curated objects from the Penroses’ global travels. At its core, three distinct dining rooms express themes of ambition and cosmopolitan sophistication through tactile metals, jewel-toned finishes, and sculptural lighting, transforming The Penrose Room into a contemporary stage for ritual and celebration. ___________________ RESTAURANT RESTAURANT BAR ___________________ CLIENT The Broadmoor visit website﻿ ___________________ OPERATOR The Broadmoor Photo Amaury Laparra Previous THE SPRINGS Next VICTORIA PLACE NEW YORK 135 West 27th Street New York, NY 10001 t. +1 212 366 5544 LEGAL privacy policy cookie policy copyright © Tihany Design

items.title: DANIEL - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design
items.text: DANIEL - Tihany Design - Luxury Interior Design DANIEL New York, NY, United States This is the second time in 11 years that the Michelin-starred Chef has entrusted Tihany Design to reconceive his stage, dining room and bar. Signature elements begin with the Chef’s cue of a red carpet-style arrival to an exquisite, polished stainless steel-arched entrance, a deliberate extension of the existing neoclassical motif of the restaurant’s interiors. Three adjacent mirrored arches segue to the redesigned lounge area with custom furnishings, ombre red carpet, a color scheme of rich grays, and a spectacular crystal-enhanced, Art Deco-inspired bar designed in partnership with Lalique. The reflectivity of the space illuminates the dialogue between past and present, providing its rich history with a delightful path forward. ___________________ RESTAURANT Michelin Rated CHEF Daniel Boulud ___________________ CLIENT Daniel Boulud ﻿visit website﻿ Photo Eric Laignel Previous PER SE Next THE BREAKERS NEW YORK 135 West 27th Street New York, NY 10001 t. +1 212 366 5544 LEGAL privacy policy cookie policy copyright © Tihany Design

items.title: Bavel — Studio UNLTD
items.text: Bavel Middle Eastern restaurants have long suffered from cliché in design aesthetics such as having a very dark, heavily patterned and often intimidating environments. The design for Bavel set out to challenge those conventions. The restaurant design embraces the influence of the regions from which the cuisine is derived (the southern Mediterranean), interpreting those ideas through the lens of its Arts District location. The worn, rather innocuous brick warehouse which houses the space, served as a wonderfully textured canvas for the restaurant to evolve from. PROJECT SUMMARY LOCATION Los Angeles, CA YEAR 2018 CLIENT Ori Menashe & Genevieve Gergis SIZE 7,200 sq. ft. interior “ In a world of excess and heaviness, this light-filled industrial space adorned with ivy is refreshing. This is handsome and well-done. ” Awards Jury Contract Magazine Natural light served as the critical ingredient employed to create a bright and inviting atmosphere. The center piece of the design is an extensive raceway of planters which hang just below the massive skylight openings, with greenery spilling over and filling the voluminous ceiling area. The primary base color in the space is white with pops of color found in tile, plaster and furnishings that are drawn from the Coastal Mediterranean-vibrant turquoise, saffron and turmeric, and patterns evoking a Moorish feel are found throughout. Seating diversity is plentiful, with a focus on comfort so diners can relax and enjoy, whether inside or on the patio. Modern and traditional styles blend to find the perfect note and finishing touch to the space.

items.title: Bar Moruno — Studio UNLTD
items.text: Bar Moruno Located along a pedestrian strip in the Silver Lake neighborhood of Los Angeles, Bar Moruno draws inspiration from the owner’s passion for Spanish tapas culture and old-world bodegas. The interior conveys a timeless sense of warmth and conviviality with echoes of 20th century sensibilities. Oversized red double doors open onto Sunset Boulevard, inviting passersby to tuck in and while the afternoon away. PROJECT SUMMARY LOCATION Los Angeles, CA YEAR 2022 CLIENT Intent To Dine SIZE 1,700 sq. ft. At the center of the space, a low partition of ribbed walnut topped with a decorative mesh screen serves the dual purpose of expanding the bar footprint with a drink rail and providing privacy to the main dining room. Diminutive, two person booths constructed of slatted walnut boast charming curves, tapered legs and paprika upholstery. Grand back bar shelving bathed in olive green provides for dramatic display of the eclectic gin and vermouth bottles at the heart of the extensive bar program. A banquette awash in turmeric gold runs the length of a salon wall displaying artwork and mirrors adding an air of authenticity that recalls family-run Spanish bodegas.

items.title: Helms Bakery — Studio UNLTD
items.text: Helms Bakery Within the historic site of the fabled Helms Bakery, which delivered its last bread in 1969, rises an adaptive reuse project undertaken by Studio UNLTD. The renovation of the 6,880 square foot bow-trussed former garage space brings to the Culver City Arts District a majestic market hall with soaring ceilings and abundant natural light. The studio employs a modern yet nostalgic design vernacular to reintroduce present-day Angelenos to the Helms brand whose identity is indelibly woven into the cultural fabric of the city. PROJECT SUMMARY LOCATION Culver City, CA 2024 6,880 sq. ft. interior | 1,000 sq. ft. exterior CLIENT Chef Sang Yoon | WNM Realty YEAR SIZE “ We wanted to work in subtle hints of the building’s history without hammering in too much art deco. We did this by layering in touches of nostalgic and traditional design elements." ” Greg Bleier Founding Principal Historic details of the building are reproduced along the new façade that match the original 1930’s construction, and custom Art-Deco pendants add to the charm. Repeated iterations of custom Art-Deco inspired arched wood “storefronts” connect the design lexicon of the bakery to the adjacent dinette.

items.title: UCHIKO MIAMI - Islyn
items.text: UCHIKO MIAMI - Islyn Projects All Projects Interior Design Branding In Development About Press & Awards Journal Contact Islyn Studio New York, NY Instagram Follow Us @islynstudio #islynstudio VIEW RECENT PROJECTS CLOSE Uchiko blends tropical brutalism with Japanese deco influences, creating a space that feels both rooted in its marina-side setting and like an enchanting escape. The design celebrates contrasts—raw and refined, bold and intimate—where handcrafted details, textured materials, and vibrant colors transport guests into a world of beauty and wonder. UCHIKO MIAMI UCHIKO MIAMI INTERIOR DESIGN READ MORE THE TUSK BAR & BRASS INTERIOR DESIGN READ MORE NOW NOW HOTEL INTERIOR DESIGN READ MORE LOCATION Miami, FL ROLE Interior Design YEAR 2025 partners Hai Hospitality City Construction Pineapple Procurement Form Group AE Design William Jess Laird SELECTED PRESS Uchiko is a poetic interpretation of Miami Beach’s spirit, blending tropical brutalism with the elegance of Japanese deco influences to create a space that feels like an escape, yet remains deeply rooted in its marina-side setting. It is a celebration of contrasts—raw and refined, bold and intimate, coastal and cosmopolitan—designed to transport guests to a world of beauty and wonder. The design of Uchiko embraces hand-crafted elements and a palette of highly textured materials and celebrates the beauty of imperfection. The material palette tells a story of the marina and its textures. Exposed concrete, softened by hand-pressed stone and shell accents, echoes the coast’s rocks where sea life finds refuge, while rich teak wood shutters add warmth and a sense of grounded elegance and tropicalism. At the entrance, the host stand is inspired by Japanese thatched roofs—setting the tone with an inviting and handcrafted feel. At the heart of the space is the signature glass block bar, a glowing jewel that captures the light of the setting sun and casts rippling reflections onto the ceiling, evoking the magic of water at golden hour. This luminous centerpiece anchors the dining room, creating an enchanting ambiance that shifts with the light as the sun sets. The color palette is a love letter to the marina’s depths, with gradients of deep blues blending seamlessly into the space. Bursts of vibrancy appear in playful artwork depicting oceanic ingredients used in the cuisine, while sea green marble mosaics are found accented in the concrete floors throughout for a modern touch. These details, paired with lush tropical plantings, bring an organic softness to the design, imbuing the space with life and vitality. The private dining room is a sanctuary within a sanctuary, an intimate retreat framed by Japanese-inspired sliding drapery and featuring a dramatic carved stone fireplace. With its moody lighting, rich textures, and enveloping warmth, the room feels like a hidden world filled with artful discoveries. Additional Japanese influences are woven throughout, from the handcrafted copper light fixtures and intricate deco-inspired drink rails to the tiled bathrooms, where rich aubergine-colored tiles immerse you in a moment of unexpected indulgence. Every element of the design feels as though it could exist nowhere else, from the tactile materials to the thoughtful craftsmanship. Uchiko embodies the essence of its setting: vibrant, layered, and timeless. It is not merely a place to dine—it is a journey through light and texture, history and innovation, sea and sky. The result is a space that invites guests to linger, discover, and connect. Whether basking in the golden glow of the bar or marveling at the interplay of textures, Uchiko leaves an indelible impression—an elevated experience that feels both effortless and extraordinary. items.text: London Scott’s Located on Mount Street, Scott’s is a 130 cover restaurant of great provenance and indisputable style. Restoring Scott's, antique charm with functional updates, without altering its unique atmosphere. Martin Brudnizki A timber panelled dining room with burgundy leather banquettes and dining chairs, silver leaf mirrored screens and a marble top with stingray fronted bar was designed. The walls are adorned with artwork from some of today’s most celebrated British artists , including Michael Landy and Gary Hume. A specific collaboration with Patrice Butler to create a bespoke chandelier was also included in the design. Further to this Amanda Levete collaborated with the Studio to design a modern crustacean display and vanity units. Selected works

items.title: Dorothee Meilichzon
items.text: Dorothee Meilichzon Menu HOTEL REGINA biarritz 52 Av. de l'Impératrice, 64200 Biarritz July 2023 Perched on a cliff in Biarritz, overlooking Cap Saint-Martin and the Atlantic Ocean, the Hôtel Regina has stood proudly for nearly 120 years. Built as a hotel in 1906 by architect Henry Martinet, the building is a remarkable example of Belle Époque architecture. This period naturally became our starting point, with its impressive 15-metre-high atrium, grand windows and sculpted architectural details. We also wanted to draw inspiration from local architectural styles of the same period, particularly Neo-Basque architecture. The work of the Gómez brothers, especially Villa Malaye, served as a reference, alongside Villa Leïhorra by Joseph Hiriart and Villa Arnaga by Albert Tournaire. These influences informed a vocabulary of white architecture, semicircular forms, sculpted frescoes, fluted cornices, 45-degree angles, tiled génoises , semicircular mirrors, black wrought iron and Art Deco stoneware tiles by Winckelmans. We also drew inspiration from the Atlantic Ocean itself: rope-inspired mouldings and skirting boards, striped fabrics, dark and pale blue lacquer finishes, ocean-liner architecture, bathroom vanities echoing the shape of a pelota pediment, and fabrics draped like sails. And, of course, shells! Razor clams are sculpted into the reception desk, while marine life appears in wall lights, carpets, fabrics and bas-reliefs. We also wanted to pay tribute to Japan and its close historical and cultural ties with the Basque Country. Japanese straw, black lacquer, indigo-dyed hanging fabrics and paper lanterns all contribute to this dialogue between cultures. The result is a luminous, layered interior where dark green, deep red and shades of blue are balanced by stoneware, ceramics and natural materials such as straw and rope. The rooms are predominantly white, blue and mint green, with undulating génoises , panelled doors, wardrobes clad in Japanese straw and rope details, and oversized headboards finished in pale blue lacquer. The corridors open onto the grand atrium and feature carpets printed with aquatic motifs. The spa combines pale blue and warm green tones, curved tiles, lime-plastered walls and straw wallcoverings. The restaurant and atrium take inspiration from the architectural language of Eileen Gray in the late 1920s. Curved wooden furniture, her iconic bar stools and a counter inspired by her house at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin evoke the streamlined elegance of a grand ocean liner. Within the atrium, we have created a series of intimate sitting areas, furnished with suspended paper lights by Ingo Maurer and Anthony Dickens, alongside sofas inspired by the forms of the Itsasoan bridge in Guéthary. items.title: Andy Baraghani’s New NYC Restaurant is Full of Design Surprises | Architectural Digest
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story “I’ve always been obsessed with design, since I was a kid,” says Andy Baraghani. “I love how restaurant interiors can take you to a different place.” At Ditto —the all-day café he is opening in New York’s Flatiron —the chef, cookbook author, and YouTube star has given that obsession free rein. With each design decision—from the vintage glass-prism Holophane pendants in the front window to the intense blue (tinted to match Benjamin Moore Buckland Blue) of the rear dining area’s Venetian plaster walls—he asked himself: “Would I actually do this in my home?” If the answer was yes, it passed the test. The interior of Ditto, with Venetian plaster walls in a shade matching Benjamin Moore Buckland Blue, and Model S22 chairs from Galvanitas. Photo: Adrian Gaut For Andy Baraghani, design is something of a family affair. His husband, Keith Pollock , is a former AD editor and now a West Elm executive. But opening a restaurant was never part of the plan. In fact, when Michael Silber, a restaurant investor behind New York hot spots like Borgo, Penny, and Bistrot Ha, approached him with the idea of a laid-back restaurant open for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, Baraghani admits his first reaction was: “I have no interest.” It wasn’t for lack of experience. He had started his career in restaurants—from Chez Panisse in Berkeley, where he worked as a teenager, to Estela in New York—before becoming a food editor at Bon Appetit and winning a James Beard Award for his cookbook, The Cook You Want to Be . But he bonded with Silber over their shared love of greenmarket cooking and decorating deep dives. When it came to Ditto, he says, he wanted the space to convey his personal style. It helped that he and Silber were on the same page. “Andy and I talked about styles ranging from Bauhaus , de Stijl , and classic modernism to 1970s and ’80s aesthetics from places like Italy and France,” Silber says. The Bauhaus-inspired counter at Ditto. Photo: Adrian Gaut They brought in like-minded collaborators: interior designer Eric Wink and architect Alta Indelman . Wink, a close friend of Baraghani who helped with the design of his and Pollock’s home, says the partners told him that New York’s much-missed City Bakery, which was two blocks uptown from Ditto’s 16th Street location, was an inspiration. “They wanted it to feel casual and approachable, with a bit of a New York diner quality,” Wink says. Holophane pendant lamps hang in the restaurant’s front window. Photo: Adrian Gaut The space, in a 1905 former factory (its last incarnation was an agnès b. store), is divided into three zones. In the front section, visitors can shop at a market area with hand-picked groceries. A glossy white counter with Bauhaus curves anchors the middle section; this is where customers line up, take a number, and either carry the food out or dine at laminate-topped tables under a trio of oversized custom fabric pendants. The menu, handwritten on a roll of butcher’s paper and updated daily, features dishes like pomegranate spoon salad and what Baraghani calls “the Platonic ideal of granola,” with tahini, maple syrup, and yogurt drizzled with fig-leaf oil. Flaky Biscuits will be a signature dish. Photo Credit: Adrian Gaut The third zone, the one painted blue, features an open kitchen and café tables pulled up to a banquette that runs the length of the room. “There’s that good chaos in the middle and the back is a calmer moment,” says Baraghani. Indelman, a veteran collaborator with New York restaurateurs like Andrew Tarlow and Gabe Stulman, was tasked with giving the space a utilitarian, high-tech ambience. She clad the walls and the open kitchen in patinated stainless steel and preserved industrial elements like structural arches and polished concrete floors. But it was Baraghani and Silber who took the lead on honing the visual details of the interiors. “We went through 50 possibilities to find the right chair,” Silber says. The one they selected—a 1960s Dutch industrial chair, the Model S22 from Galvanitas —was sourced from Amsterdam Modern in Los Angeles. Silber also spent hours on eBay bidding on midcentury ceramic bud vases. “They were each under $20 but put them together on a shelf and you have your own little Giorgio Morandi tableau,” he says. White wall speakers and a French ceramic mask hang above the banquette, tables, and stools upholstered in Maharam’s Stripe It fabric. The no-nonsense decor also features white wall speakers, created for the space by sound artist Tom Bloxam , and programmed with playlists created by Michael Scanlon of Chandelier Creative , which oversaw Ditto’s branding. But there are quirkier moments too. When it came to choosing fabric for the custom stools, Baraghani insisted on Maharam’s Stripe It , which he felt had a “Baja California” vibe. “We needed that twist,” he says. For his part, Wink specified his favorite stainless-steel toilet for the restrooms— Neo-Metro’s wall-mounted MiniLoo . “I added a custom wood top to soften it a bit,” Wink says. Meanwhile, a pair of massive midcentury French ceramic faces that hang on a wall opposite the menu of the day are on loan from Baraghani’s own home. “They anchor the space and add a touch of craft,” he says. “I just knew they needed to be here.”

SILVER LAKE POOL & INN SILVER LAKE, CA, 2019 SILVER LAKE POOL & INN SILVER LAKE, CA, 2019 photography courtesy of palisociety Inspired by Silver Lake’s historical legacy as a magnet for iconoclasts and its reputation as the Bohemian epicenter of Los Angeles. The warm and sunny climate, over 50 storybook staircases knitting the lush hills together, and the eclectic personalities of locals that Silver Lake Pool & Inn would soon attract all contributed to the design elements and overarching desire to create an informal and melodious meeting place in the neighborhood. In addition to Silver Lake’s history and natural landscaping, inspiration came from a myriad of eclectic sources. The work of Luis Barragán, a pioneer of Mexican Modernism, was frequently referenced for his genius in eliciting tranquility from clean lines, natural materials, color and use of light. This feeling was achieved through our use of natural, handmade and vintage elements, sunset tones and open, inviting spaces, ultimately creating a place to connect, create and relax. The Southern California climate allowed for most social spaces to be outdoors, with intimate and casual seating in the garden-like atmosphere within verdant, cascading terraces joined together by exterior staircases, echoing the local context. Flagstone flooring and handmade Moroccan and Italian tilework within tree-covered courtyards create intimate oases in which locals and tourists alike find themselves at ease and refreshed. Electric Bowery tied the exterior spaces together with smooth finish plaster & vintage stucco, paying homage to the Mexican influence on Southern Californian architecture. Within the hotel guest rooms, a warm and singularly Californian ethos was achieved through custom millwork, handmade Moroccan tile, and terrazzo nightstands and vanities commissioned by Concrete Collaborative. A sense of spaciousness and warmth was achieved by optimizing natural light and supplementing with vintage-inspired floor lamps, sconces and fixtures by ANDlight. Armchairs made of leather and wood, prints by Blockshop and Alexandra Berg, and Laure Joliet photography animate the space while live plants and antique rugs unique to each room accomplish our desire for every guest to experience subtly distinct decorative elements. A cactus garden inset within the hotel and exterior stairways connecting the outside terraces blur the line between exterior and interior space, creating a social sanctuary within the urban Silver Lake context. items.title: CHLEO - Islyn
items.text: CHLEO - Islyn Projects All Projects Interior Design Branding In Development About Press & Awards Journal Contact Islyn Studio New York, NY Instagram Follow Us @islynstudio #islynstudio VIEW RECENT PROJECTS CLOSE The remnants of a fire’s past leaves a mark on human experience. Charred ash and the single plume of smoke from a cooling flame indicate the presence of a gathering, a fleeting moment in time. The physicality of fire helps to tell our stories and was the inspiration behind the design for Chleo; a wine bar in Kingston, NY. CHLEO UCHIKO MIAMI INTERIOR DESIGN READ MORE THE TUSK BAR & BRASS INTERIOR DESIGN READ MORE NOW NOW HOTEL INTERIOR DESIGN READ MORE LOCATION Kingston, NY ROLE Interior Design YEAR 2023 partners Hope and Charles Matthews SELECTED PRESS Inspired by fire, wine, and nourishment – the first things that brought people together – Chleo boils hospitality down to its roots, offering unparalleled service and a second home for a growing neighborhood. Aiming to shift the status quo and create a more equitable and sustainable future, the client’s objective for their first self-owned restaurant in Kingston, NY was to offer the experience of fine dining while stripping away the formality, structure, and elitism that makes it hard to reach. Their mission extended in celebrating the bounty and people of the Hudson Valley, in an effort to connect with the land and those who cultivate it. To support this, we sought to create a space that fosters genuine human connections and memorable experiences with a giving spirit. The restaurant is meant to serve as a diplomatic space for people to reconnect and appreciate the simple joys of a beautiful meal; a respite that pulls cues from Hudson Valley’s life-giving environs and traditions of craftsmanship. For the interior design visioning, we went back to where we started – the hearth – which has long stood as the cornerstone of a home, fostering togetherness. With meticulously considered design, we transformed a forlorn space into moments of discovery through the story of fire. A dark open kitchen against a pale grey limewash nods to the nuanced idea of charred ash and plumes of smoke from a cooling flame – the presence of gatherings past. Carefully placed mirrors animate the energy and flame of the kitchen, no matter where you’re sitting. Foraged and dried seasonal ingredients hang on display and find their way on your plate, offering an intimate connection to the pleasures of Hudson Valley bounty. Hand-carved wood detailing proudly displays the irregularities of spalted maple harvested less than 100 miles away. Every detail of the space is meant to draw you in, create conversation, and provide an experience that could only exist on that particular corner of Kingston. Beyond aesthetics, we were inspired by the chef’s unrelenting commitment to honest sustainability, and saw an opportunity to usher in a new and better era at a human scale. The project bears regional materials and products to form a hyper-localized space; by sourcing through local means, we not only created a space full of nostalgic materials and familiar forms, but worked to amplify the voices of Hudson Valley’s artists, florists, and makers to create a unique sense of renewability within the community. Chleo is a testament to collaboration, conversation, and discovery; an idiosyncratic vessel for expression and innovation, made by and for the locals. Anticipating the needs of a modern era, the spirit of the restaurant believes that a brightly prepared meal and the place with which you enjoy it go far beyond the visual or the taste. It’s something you can feel. PREVIOUS PROJECT NEXT PROJECT
